controls.title: Delegate administration to per-service groups, not one blanket tenancy admin group
controls.objective: Routine operation of individual OCI services should be performed by groups whose grants are scoped to a single service family and a single compartment subtree, so that compromise or error inside one service cannot be leveraged into tenancy-wide control. Concentrating all operational work in the tenancy Administrators group removes any blast-radius boundary.
controls.procedure: Enumerate all ACTIVE compartments with `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all`. Note that `--include-root` is a valueless switch: writing `--include-root true` aborts the command with an unexpected-argument error, and omitting it drops the root compartment where most tenancy-scoped policies live. For each compartment OCID run `oci iam policy list --compartment-id <id> --all`, then `oci iam policy get --policy-id <id>` to read the `statements` array, and build a matrix of subject group -> verb -> resource-family -> scope. Derive the set of service families actually in use deterministically rather than by opinion: run `oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query all resources" --region <region>` once for every region returned by `oci iam region-subscription list`, then map each returned `resource-type` to its policy family (instance -> instance-family, bucket -> object-family, volume -> volume-family, vcn/subnet/securitylist -> virtual-network-family, autonomousdatabase -> database-family, functionsfunction -> functions-family, and so on). Cross-reference the policy subjects with `oci iam group list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all` and, per identity domain, `oci identity-domains groups list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query all resources" --region <region> --query 'data.items[]."resource-type"'
controls.evidence: The `statements` string array from each `oci iam policy get` response, keyed by policy OCID and its `compartment-id`; the group name/OCID list from `oci iam group list` and per-domain `oci identity-domains groups list`; and the derived in-use family table (distinct `resource-type` values per region from `oci search resource structured-search`, with the family each maps to).
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every service family in the set derived from the per-region Resource Search inventory, at least one group other than Administrators holds a compartment-scoped manage grant on that family, and no group outside Administrators holds `manage all-resources in tenancy`. If the derived in-use set is empty for a region the run is inconclusive, not a PASS.
controls.remediation: Create one group per service function (for example storage operators, network operators, database operators) and write policies of the form `allow group <name> to manage <service>-family in compartment <compartment>`. In a multi-domain tenancy qualify the subject as `allow group '<DomainName>'/'<GroupName>' to ...`. Remove those individuals from Administrators and keep Administrators for break-glass only. Attach `where` conditions on `request.permission` to narrow the grant further where the service supports it.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because no API can tell whether the observed split of duties matches the organisation's operating model — a tenancy with three service groups may still be non-compliant if one of them is a de-facto super-admin. Automation traps: (1) `--include-root` takes no value, so the common `--include-root true` form fails outright and a silent fallback to a root-only listing misses most policies, since policies are created in any compartment; (2) in multi-domain tenancies policy subjects are written as `group '<DomainName>'/'<GroupName>'`, so string matching on `group <name>` silently misses every non-Default-domain grant; (3) Resource Search is a regional, eventually-consistent, permission-filtered index — a single-region run yields a short in-use family set and the rule then passes vacuously, so loop every subscribed region and treat a caller with partial inspect permission as inconclusive rather than compliant.

controls.title: Unbounded tenancy authority stays with the break-glass admin group alone
controls.objective: A statement that grants manage on all-resources at tenancy scope is equivalent to full tenancy ownership: it covers IAM, keys, audit configuration and every workload. Only the built-in Administrators group should hold it, so that the set of principals with unbounded authority is small, known, and monitorable.
controls.procedure: Walk the full compartment tree with `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all` (`--include-root` is a valueless switch — do not pass it a value, and do not omit it, because `in tenancy` statements can only live in the root compartment). List policies in each compartment and pull `statements` via `oci iam policy get --policy-id`. Normalise each statement to lowercase and tokenise subject / verb / resource / scope rather than substring-matching. Flag any statement whose resource is `all-resources`, whose verb is `manage`, whose scope is `in tenancy`, and whose subject is anything other than the built-in Administrators group — including `any-user`, `dynamic-group`, and domain-qualified `group '<Domain>'/'<Name>'` subjects. Resource Search may be used only to accelerate discovery, and then only against the home region resolved from `oci iam region-subscription list`, because IAM objects are home-region/global while the Search endpoint is regional.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query policy resources" --region <home_region> --query 'data.items[].{id:identifier,c:"compartment-id"}'
controls.evidence: Each offending element of the `statements` array returned by `oci iam policy get --policy-id`, quoted verbatim together with the policy OCID, policy name and owning `compartment-id`; plus the Administrators group OCID from `oci iam group list` used to establish which subject is exempt.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no policy statement in any compartment grants manage on all-resources in tenancy to a subject other than the built-in Administrators group (no any-user, no dynamic-group, no other named or domain-qualified group). A run whose compartment enumeration did not include the root compartment, or that relied solely on Resource Search, is inconclusive and may not be recorded as PASS.
controls.remediation: Delete or rewrite the offending statement. Replace the tenancy-wide grant with the narrowest scope that still works: pin the verb to `use` or `read` where possible, pin the resource to a specific family such as `instance-family` or `object-family`, and pin the scope to `in compartment <name>`. If a broad grant is genuinely needed, bound it with `where` conditions on `request.permission` or `request.region`.
controls.caveat: Only a root-compartment policy can carry `in tenancy` scope, but you must still read child-compartment policies: `manage all-resources in compartment <top-level-compartment>` over a compartment holding 95% of the estate is a near-equivalent grant that a regex looking for the literal `in tenancy` will pass. Two command-level false passes: `--include-root true` aborts the compartment walk (the flag takes no value), and running `oci search resource structured-search` without `--region <home_region>` queries a regional index that holds no home-region IAM objects, returning an empty item list that reads as 'no offending statements' on the most severe control in the section — confirm `policy` is even an indexed type with `oci search resource-type list` before leaning on it, and keep the compartment-tree walk as the authoritative enumeration. Statement text is free-form: case varies, several subjects may be comma-separated in one statement, and a trailing `where` clause may or may not constrain it, so token parsing beats substring matching. Search results are also eventually consistent and filtered by the caller's inspect permission.

controls.title: Fence identity administrators out of the Administrators group via policy conditions
controls.objective: Delegated identity administrators need to create users and groups, but if they can also modify membership of the tenancy Administrators group they can escalate themselves to full tenancy control at will. The grant must therefore carry an explicit condition that excludes the Administrators group as a target.
controls.procedure: Enumerate policies across the whole compartment tree (`oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all`, with `--include-root` passed as a bare switch) and read `statements` with `oci iam policy get --policy-id`. Select every statement whose subject is not the Administrators group and whose resource is `groups`, `users`, `policies`, `all-resources`, or an identity aggregate, with verb `use` or `manage` (these resources exist only at tenancy scope, so the scope will read `in tenancy`). For each, verify the statement carries a `where` clause containing a `target.group.name` inequality naming the admin group, commonly inside `where all { ... }`. Separately, per identity domain resolved from `oci iam domain list`, enumerate administrator application-role grants with `oci identity-domains grants list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` (optionally filtered with `--filter 'app.value eq "<idcs_admin_app_id>"'`) and resolve the role names via `oci identity-domains app-roles list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`, to catch escalation paths that bypass IAM policy entirely.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The verbatim statement string from `oci iam policy get --policy-id`, showing presence or absence of a `where ... target.group.name != 'Administrators'` condition, keyed by policy OCID and compartment OCID; plus the grantee list from `oci identity-domains grants list --endpoint <domain_url>` joined to `oci identity-domains app-roles list` so each grant is named (Identity Domain Administrator, User Administrator, Security Administrator) and attributed to a group or user.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every statement granting use or manage on groups, users, policies or all-resources at tenancy scope to a non-Administrators subject includes a condition excluding `target.group.name` equal to the admin group name, and no group or user outside the intended tenancy-administrator set holds a domain administrator application role in any identity domain.
controls.remediation: Rewrite the grant as `allow group <IdentityAdmins> to manage groups in tenancy where all {target.group.name != 'Administrators'}`, and apply the same pattern to the `users` and `policies` resource types. Where a second identity domain has its own Administrators group, add an inequality for that name too (domain-qualified subjects and targets must be written explicitly). Review domain-level application role grants with `oci identity-domains grants list` and revoke Identity Domain Administrator, User Administrator and Security Administrator from any group that is not intended to be tenancy-equivalent.
controls.caveat: The biggest false pass is checking IAM policy alone. In an identity-domain tenancy the domain's own administrator application roles (Identity Domain Administrator, User Administrator, Security Administrator) are granted through SCIM grants, not IAM policies, and confer group-management power that no `where target.group.name` condition constrains — so `grants list` is mandatory, not supplementary. The condition value is also matched on the group name exactly as written: a tenancy that renamed or duplicated the admin group, or that has an Administrators group in a second identity domain, is not protected by a condition naming only the Default-domain string. Statements granting `manage all-resources` implicitly include the groups resource type and must be selected too. Finally the compartment walk must use `--include-root` as a bare switch — `--include-root true` fails the command outright, and a root-less walk misses the tenancy-scoped statements this control is about.

controls.title: Require at least 14 characters in every effective identity domain password policy
controls.objective: Password length is the dominant factor in resistance to offline cracking and online guessing for locally managed accounts. Every password policy that can apply to a local user in any identity domain must enforce a minimum length of at least 14 characters, not just the policy named Default.
controls.procedure: List identity domains across the compartment tree: `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all` (bare `--include-root` switch), then `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all` capturing each domain's `url`. For every domain run `oci identity-domains password-policies list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` — the identity-domains CLI uses the plural SCIM resource name for list operations, so the singular `password-policy list` does not exist — and read `min-length` on each entry of `data.resources[]`, together with `priority` and the `groups` assignment that determines who it applies to. Use the singular form only for single-resource operations (`oci identity-domains password-policy get --password-policy-id <id>`). For a legacy (pre-domain) tenancy also run `oci iam authentication-policy get --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid>`.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The `min-length` attribute of every PasswordPolicy in `data.resources[]` returned by `oci identity-domains password-policies list --endpoint <domain_url>`, recorded with the policy `display-name`, its `priority`, its assigned `groups`, and the domain OCID; for legacy tenancies, `data.password-policy.minimum-password-length` from `oci iam authentication-policy get`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every password policy in every identity domain of the tenancy reports min-length >= 14, and, where the legacy authentication policy exists, password-policy.minimum-password-length >= 14. A domain enumeration that did not walk the compartment subtree is inconclusive, not a PASS.
controls.remediation: Raise the minimum on each policy with a SCIM patch: `oci identity-domains password-policy patch --endpoint <domain_url> --password-policy-id <id> --schemas '["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"]' --operations '[{"op":"replace","path":"minLength","value":14}]'` (patch paths use camelCase SCIM attribute names; `password-policy put` also works but replaces the whole object and therefore needs every required attribute restated). Do this for every policy in the domain, not only the default one, and repeat per identity domain. Where a lower-length policy exists solely for a legacy application, retire the application rather than the length requirement.
controls.caveat: Four false-pass traps. (1) A domain can hold several password policies ordered by `priority` and bound to groups; the policy that actually applies to a given user is the highest-priority matching one, so inspecting only the policy named Default can pass a tenancy whose real users are governed by a weaker one. (2) Identity domains are compartment-scoped resources — a domain created in a child compartment is invisible to `oci iam domain list -c <tenancy_ocid>` alone, so the subtree walk is mandatory, and that walk requires `--include-root` written as a bare switch because `--include-root true` aborts the command and can leave an automated collector with an empty domain list that scores as compliant. (3) The list verb is plural (`password-policies list`); the singular form errors out, and a script that swallows the non-zero exit reads 'no policies' as 'no violations'. (4) Federated users authenticate at the external IdP and are not governed by the domain password policy at all; their length requirement must be evidenced at the IdP and is out of scope for this API check.

controls.title: Force periodic password rotation with an expiry no longer than one year
controls.objective: A local account password that never expires stays valid indefinitely after a breach, a device compromise or an employee departure that HR offboarding missed. Bounding the lifetime of every locally managed password limits how long a silently stolen credential remains usable.
controls.procedure: Walk the compartment tree (`oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all`, with `--include-root` as a valueless switch), collect every identity domain URL with `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, then for each domain run `oci identity-domains password-policies list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` (plural for list operations) and read `password-expires-after` (days) on each entry of `data.resources[]` alongside `priority` and its group assignment. Determine, for each population of local users, which policy wins on priority. For legacy tenancies check `oci iam authentication-policy get --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid>`, which exposes no expiry field and therefore cannot satisfy this control by itself.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The `password-expires-after` value of each PasswordPolicy in `data.resources[]` from `oci identity-domains password-policies list --endpoint <domain_url>`, captured with the policy `display-name`, `priority` and the domain OCID, plus the list of groups the policy is scoped to.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every password policy that can apply to a local (non-federated) user sets password-expires-after to a value greater than 0 and less than or equal to 365 days; a null, absent or 0 value (never expires) is a FAIL. A policy assigned to no groups is recorded as ineffective and cannot be used to satisfy the rule for any user population.
controls.remediation: Set an expiry on each policy in each domain: `oci identity-domains password-policy patch --endpoint <domain_url> --password-policy-id <id> --schemas '["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"]' --operations '[{"op":"replace","path":"passwordExpiresAfter","value":365},{"op":"replace","path":"passwordExpireWarning","value":15}]'`. Pair the expiry with a warning window so users rotate before lockout, and confirm that service accounts using passwords are migrated to API keys or instance principals so that expiry does not break automation.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual: the API returns the setting on each policy but not which policy governs which human. A person must decide whether every population of local accounts is actually covered — including accounts in secondary identity domains, accounts exempted by a higher-priority policy bound to a group, and break-glass accounts that teams often deliberately exclude. Command-level traps that produce a silent empty result set (and therefore a vacuous pass): `--include-root` must be a bare switch, and the list verb must be the plural `password-policies list`. The API also cannot settle the federated case: for IdP-managed users the OCI value is irrelevant and the effective expiry lives in the external directory, which must be evidenced separately. Finally, a policy with a compliant expiry that is assigned to no groups changes nothing and still reads as compliant field-by-field.

controls.title: Block reuse of recent passwords by keeping a password history in each domain policy
controls.objective: Expiry only helps if users cannot cycle straight back to the password an attacker already holds. Retaining a history of previous passwords and refusing to accept them forces genuinely new secrets at each rotation, which is what makes the expiry control in 1.5 meaningful.
controls.procedure: For every identity domain found by walking the compartment tree (`oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all`, bare `--include-root`) and calling `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, run `oci identity-domains password-policies list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` and read `num-passwords-in-history` on each entry of `data.resources[]`, together with `priority` and the groups it is assigned to. Confirm the value on every policy, not just the highest-priority one, since a lower-priority policy still governs the users it matches. Legacy tenancies expose no equivalent field on `oci iam authentication-policy get`.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The `num-passwords-in-history` attribute of every PasswordPolicy in `data.resources[]` returned by `oci identity-domains password-policies list --endpoint <domain_url>`, recorded per policy `display-name`, `priority`, assigned groups and domain OCID.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every password policy that can apply to a local user reports num-passwords-in-history >= 24; a null, absent, or 0 value is a FAIL, and any value between 1 and 23 is a FAIL for this rule. A policy bound to no groups is recorded as ineffective and does not satisfy the rule for any population.
controls.remediation: Raise the history depth on each policy: `oci identity-domains password-policy patch --endpoint <domain_url> --password-policy-id <id> --schemas '["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"]' --operations '[{"op":"replace","path":"numPasswordsInHistory","value":24}]'`, repeating for every policy in every identity domain. Combine with a minimum password age (`minPasswordAge`) so a user cannot burn through the history in a single sitting to return to a favoured password.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual: the assessor must judge whether the configured depth is meaningful for the population it governs, and whether every population is governed at all. Automated traps: policies in secondary identity domains living in child compartments are missed unless the compartment tree is walked with `--include-root` as a valueless switch (passing it a value aborts the command); the list verb is the plural `password-policies list`, and the singular form errors out so a script that ignores the exit status sees zero policies and reports no violations; a policy carrying a compliant history value but assigned to zero groups is cosmetic; and a high-priority weaker policy bound to a broad group overrides compliant lower-priority ones for most users. Federated users never touch this setting — their reuse control sits in the external IdP and cannot be evidenced from OCI. History depth also does not prevent trivially incremented passwords.

controls.title: Require a second authentication factor for every account that can sign in to the Console
controls.objective: A Console password alone is phishable and reusable. Every account capable of interactive sign-in must present a second factor, so that a stolen or guessed password does not by itself yield an authenticated session with whatever OCI authority that account holds.
controls.procedure: Determine the home region with `oci iam region-subscription list`. Walk the compartment tree (`oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all`, bare `--include-root`) and collect every domain URL via `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`. For each domain run `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all --attribute-sets all` and read, per user in `data.resources[]`: `active`, the capabilities extension flag for console password use, the user extension flag indicating a federated account, and the MFA extension `mfaStatus`. Then enumerate sign-on policies and rules with the plural list verbs `oci identity-domains policies list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` and `oci identity-domains rules list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`. Order the SignOn rules by `priority`, take the first enabled rule whose condition group evaluates true for the all-users case, and inspect its `return`/action values to establish whether a second factor is demanded.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: Per user from `oci identity-domains users list`: `active`, `urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:oracle:idcs:extension:capabilities:User.canUseConsolePassword`, `...:extension:user:User.isFederatedUser` and `...:extension:mfa:User.mfaStatus` (the CLI kebab-cases sub-attributes in output, e.g. `"...:extension:mfa:User"."mfa-status"`). Plus, from `oci identity-domains policies list` and `oci identity-domains rules list`, the SignOn policy name, each rule's `priority`, `active` flag, `condition`/condition-group and its `return` action values, and the app the policy is attached to.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when both conjuncts hold. (a) Every ACTIVE non-federated user whose canUseConsolePassword capability is true reports mfaStatus ENROLLED. (b) In each identity domain, walking that domain's SignOn policy rules in ascending `priority` order, the first enabled rule whose condition group matches the all-users case has an action requiring a second factor; if that first matching rule allows authentication without a factor, the control FAILs regardless of enrolment. A domain whose SignOn policy is not attached to the Console application is a FAIL for (b).
controls.remediation: Create or edit the domain's sign-on policy so the highest-priority rule matching all users has an action requiring multi-factor authentication, confirm the policy is attached to the Console application, and have each enrolled user register a factor. For accounts that exist only for API use, clear the console-password capability instead (`oci iam user update-user-capabilities --user-id <ocid> --can-use-console-password false`, or the domain-side capabilities patch) so they cannot sign in interactively at all.
controls.caveat: The legacy `is-mfa-activated` field on `oci iam user list` is a false-pass and false-fail generator: it only reflects the Default identity domain, ignores every secondary domain entirely, and historically tracks only the legacy TOTP factor, so a user secured with a FIDO security key can report false — do not use it as evidence. The inverse trap is worse: mfaStatus ENROLLED proves a factor was registered, not that it is ever demanded, so the rule check is not optional, and it must be resolved by `priority` order with the first matching enabled rule winning rather than by 'some rule somewhere requires MFA' — an MFA rule sitting below a broader allow-without-MFA rule never fires. A sign-on policy that requires MFA but is not attached to the Console application likewise protects nothing. The list verbs are plural (`policies list`, `rules list`); the singular forms do not exist and their error exit can be mistaken for an empty, compliant result. Federated users are challenged by the external IdP, so their OCI MFA fields are meaningless and must be evidenced at the IdP.

controls.title: No API signing key stays in service past a 90-day lifetime
controls.objective: An API signing key is a long-lived bearer credential: anyone holding the private half can call OCI as that user from anywhere, with no second factor and no session expiry. Bounding key lifetime bounds how long an undetected key theft remains exploitable.
controls.procedure: Work against the home region resolved from `oci iam region-subscription list`. Enumerate users in every identity domain: walk the compartment tree (`oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all`), resolve each domain URL with `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, then `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`; for the Default domain also `oci iam user list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all`. For each user OCID run `oci iam user api-key list --user-id <ocid>`, or list a whole domain in one call with the plural verb `oci identity-domains api-keys list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`. Read `fingerprint` as the key identifier — `key-id` is the composite `<tenancy_ocid>/<user_ocid>/<fingerprint>` string, not the fingerprint — and compute each key's age from its creation timestamp against the assessment date.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: For each key: `fingerprint` (the identifier the delete command consumes), optionally `key-id` for the composite form, `time-created` (legacy) or `meta.created` (domain SCIM), `lifecycle-state`, and the owning user OCID, as returned by `oci iam user api-key list --user-id` or `oci identity-domains api-keys list`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every API key in ACTIVE state, across every user in every identity domain, has a creation timestamp no more than 90 days before the assessment timestamp. A run that enumerated users only through legacy `oci iam user list` is inconclusive, not a PASS, because it covers the Default domain only.
controls.remediation: Generate a fresh key pair, upload the new public key with `oci iam user api-key upload --user-id <ocid> --key-file <new_public.pem>`, roll the consumers over to the new fingerprint, then delete the old one with `oci iam user api-key delete --user-id <ocid> --fingerprint <old_fingerprint>` (domain equivalent: `oci identity-domains api-key delete --endpoint <domain_url> --api-key-id <id>`). Automate the cycle on a schedule under 90 days, and prefer instance or resource principals for workloads so no key exists to rotate.
controls.caveat: There is no rotation timestamp in OCI — rotation is delete-and-recreate, so creation time is the only truth, and a key re-uploaded with the same fingerprint still reads as new. Three collection traps. (1) `key-id` is not the fingerprint: it is `<tenancy>/<user>/<fingerprint>`, so keying evidence on it produces an identifier that `api-key delete --fingerprint` will not accept and that will not join to audit records. (2) Scope: `oci iam user list -c <tenancy_ocid>` returns only Default-domain principals, so every key held by a user in a secondary identity domain goes uncounted unless you enumerate domains across the whole compartment subtree (with `--include-root` as a bare switch) and query each domain endpoint with the plural `api-keys list`. (3) Users are global/home-region objects, so do not loop regions, but do run the read against the home region. Keys on deprovisioned users still authenticate until deleted.

controls.title: Replace S3-compatible customer secret keys at least every 90 days
controls.objective: Customer secret keys are static access-key/secret pairs used by the Object Storage S3-compatibility and Swift endpoints. They are frequently embedded in backup jobs and third-party appliances, where they leak into config files and images, so their useful lifetime must be capped.
controls.procedure: Against the home region, enumerate every user in every identity domain: walk compartments with `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all` (`--include-root` takes no value), get domain URLs with `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, list users per domain with `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`, plus `oci iam user list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all` for the Default domain. For each user run `oci iam customer-secret-key list --user-id <ocid>`, or take the whole domain at once with the plural verb `oci identity-domains customer-secret-keys list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`. Age each key from its creation timestamp against the assessment date.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The `time-created` / `meta.created`, `time-expires` where present, and `lifecycle-state` of each customer secret key, keyed by secret-key OCID (or SCIM id), `display-name` and owning user OCID, from `oci iam customer-secret-key list --user-id` or `oci identity-domains customer-secret-keys list`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every customer secret key in ACTIVE state, across every user in every identity domain, has a creation timestamp no more than 90 days before the assessment timestamp. A run whose user inventory came only from legacy `oci iam user list` is inconclusive, not a PASS.
controls.remediation: Create the replacement first with `oci iam customer-secret-key create --user-id <ocid> --display-name <name>`, capture the secret shown once, repoint the S3/Swift clients, then delete the superseded key with `oci iam customer-secret-key delete --user-id <ocid> --customer-secret-key-id <id>`. Where the consumer runs on OCI compute, migrate it to native Object Storage APIs with instance principals so no static pair is needed.
controls.caveat: The API never returns the secret half and exposes no last-used field, so age is the only signal available here — proving a stale key is unused requires correlating Object Storage access logs, which is control 1.16's job, not this one, and note that S3-compatible traffic is data-plane, so it does not appear in the audit stream unless bucket read/write logs are enabled. As with API keys, enumerating users only through legacy `oci iam user list` silently omits every secondary identity domain and yields a false pass, and the domain-side list verb is the plural `customer-secret-keys list` — the singular form errors, which an unchecked script reads as 'no keys'. The compartment walk needs `--include-root` written as a bare switch; `--include-root true` aborts it. Finally, these keys authenticate against the regional S3-compatibility endpoint of the Object Storage namespace, so a key created for one region works tenancy-wide: deleting it once is sufficient, but scoping the assessment per-region is not.

controls.title: Auth tokens are reissued before they reach 90 days old
controls.objective: Auth tokens are Oracle-generated passwords used by services that cannot perform request signing — Container Registry logins, Git clients for DevOps repositories, and Swift/RMAN backups to Object Storage. They are pasted into CI configuration and developer machines, so a fixed maximum lifetime limits exposure from leaked pipeline definitions. Note that Email Delivery uses a different object entirely (SMTP credentials, listed with `oci iam smtp-credential list --user-id <ocid>` or the domain-side `smtp-credentials list`), which this control does not enumerate and which must be aged separately.
controls.procedure: Against the home region, build the full user inventory: walk the compartment tree with `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all` (valueless `--include-root`), resolve each identity domain URL with `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, list users per domain with `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`, and include `oci iam user list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all`. For each user run `oci iam auth-token list --user-id <ocid>`, or enumerate the whole domain with the plural verb `oci identity-domains auth-tokens list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`. Compare each token's creation timestamp to the assessment date.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
oci iam smtp-credential list --user-id <user_ocid> --query 'data[].{id:id,created:"time-created"}'  # separate credential type, assessed alongside
controls.evidence: The `time-created` / `meta.created`, `lifecycle-state` and description of each auth token, keyed by token OCID (or SCIM id) and owning user OCID, from `oci iam auth-token list --user-id` or `oci identity-domains auth-tokens list`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every auth token in ACTIVE state, across every user in every identity domain, has a creation timestamp no more than 90 days before the assessment timestamp. Every token on a user is assessed, not just the most recent one; a run limited to legacy `oci iam user list` is inconclusive, not a PASS.
controls.remediation: Issue the replacement with `oci iam auth-token create --user-id <ocid> --description <purpose>`, store the value shown once in a Vault secret rather than in pipeline files, update the consumers, then delete the old token with `oci iam auth-token delete --user-id <ocid> --auth-token-id <id>`. Each user is capped at two tokens, which is exactly enough for a make-before-break rotation, so the deletion must be the final scripted step rather than a manual follow-up.
controls.caveat: Because a user may hold at most two auth tokens, teams often keep a permanent spare that never gets deleted after a rotation — it reads as a valid credential and is the most common finding here, so assess every token, not the newest one. Enumerating users only via legacy `oci iam user list` misses secondary identity domains entirely, and the domain-side list verb is the plural `auth-tokens list`; the singular form does not exist and its error can be swallowed as an empty, compliant result. The compartment walk needs `--include-root` as a bare switch. Do not assume this control covers Email Delivery: SMTP credentials are a distinct object that none of these commands return, so a tenancy with ancient SMTP credentials passes this control cleanly. Tokens also survive deactivation of the console password: disabling interactive login does not revoke them, so an offboarded user whose password was removed may still be able to push to Container Registry until the token itself is deleted.

controls.title: Replace IAM database credentials at least every 90 days
controls.objective: IAM database passwords let an OCI principal authenticate directly to Autonomous Database and other managed databases, bridging cloud identity into data-plane access. A stale one is a long-lived path to customer data that never appears in database-side user administration, so its lifetime must be bounded.
controls.procedure: Against the home region, inventory users across all identity domains: `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all` (`--include-root` is valueless), then `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, then `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` per domain, plus `oci iam user list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all`. For each user run `oci iam db-credential list --user-id <ocid>`, or take the domain in one call with the plural verb `oci identity-domains user-db-credentials list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`. Record each credential's creation timestamp and its expiry, then age it against the assessment date.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The `time-created`, `time-expires` and `lifecycle-state` of each DB credential from `oci iam db-credential list --user-id <ocid>`, keyed by credential OCID and owning user OCID (SCIM equivalents from `oci identity-domains user-db-credentials list`: `meta.created`, `expires-on`).
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every DB credential in ACTIVE state, across every user in every identity domain, has a creation timestamp no more than 90 days before the assessment timestamp and is not already past its expiry while still ACTIVE. A user inventory drawn only from legacy `oci iam user list` is inconclusive, not a PASS.
controls.remediation: Rotate by delete-and-recreate on a schedule under 90 days: create the replacement with `oci iam db-credential create --user-id <ocid> --password <value> --description <purpose>`, repoint the database clients, then delete the superseded credential with `oci iam db-credential delete --user-id <ocid> --db-credential-id <id>`. Do not attempt to set a lifetime on the legacy create call — it has no expiry parameter and `time-expires` is service-populated. In an identity-domain tenancy the expiry is writable on the SCIM object instead: create or replace the UserDbCredential through `oci identity-domains user-db-credentials create` / `oci identity-domains user-db-credential put` with `expiresOn` set. Prefer database resource principals or Vault-brokered secrets for application connections.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because IAM only shows that a credential object exists — it cannot show whether any database actually trusts it. The IAM-to-database mapping is configured on the database side (the global/shared schema mapping in Autonomous Database), so a human must confirm, per database, whether an aged credential still grants a working login and what schema privileges it lands on; an unmapped credential is dormant while a mapped one is a direct data path. Second trap: an ACTIVE credential whose `time-expires` has already passed is refused by the database but still listed by IAM, so counting objects overstates the finding unless expiry is evaluated too. Third: the remediation must not promise an expiry the legacy API cannot set — `db-credential create` exposes no expiry parameter, and only the identity-domains UserDbCredential object accepts `expiresOn`, so a runbook that tells an operator to 'set a 90-day expiry' on the legacy path silently leaves the default in place. Secondary-domain users are missed by legacy user enumeration, and these credentials produce no OCI control-plane audit events, so idleness for them must come from database-side audit (see 1.16).

controls.title: Deny long-lived signing keys to accounts holding tenancy administrator rights
controls.objective: Administrator accounts should only be usable interactively, behind MFA. An API signing key attached to such an account is an unattended, non-MFA, non-expiring path to full tenancy control that survives password rotation and is invisible to sign-on policy, which is precisely the combination an attacker wants.
controls.procedure: Resolve the Administrators group OCID from `oci iam group list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all`, then list its members with `oci iam group list-users --group-id <ocid> --all`. In every identity domain, repeat with the domain's own Administrators group: `oci identity-domains groups list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` to find it, then `oci identity-domains group get --endpoint <domain_url> --group-id <id> --attributes members`, because membership is not returned by default and `--attribute-sets all` alone does not populate it. Extend the set with members of any group that policy analysis (control 1.2) showed holds `manage all-resources in tenancy`, and with holders of domain administrator application roles from `oci identity-domains grants list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`. For every user in that combined set run `oci iam user api-key list --user-id <ocid>` (or the domain-side `oci identity-domains api-keys list --endpoint <domain_url> --all` filtered to that user) and confirm the result is empty.
controls.evidence: An empty (or non-empty) `data` array from `oci iam user api-key list --user-id <admin_user_ocid>`, with each key identified by its `fingerprint` and `time-created`; paired with the membership listing that establishes the user is an administrator — `oci iam group list-users --group-id <administrators_group_ocid>`, the `members` attribute from `oci identity-domains group get --attributes members`, the qualifying statement text from `oci iam policy get`, and the admin role grants from `oci identity-domains grants list`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every user who is a member of any Administrators group in any identity domain, of any group granted manage all-resources in tenancy, or holding a domain administrator application role, returns zero ACTIVE API keys. A membership enumeration that did not request the `members` attribute, or that covered only the Default domain, is inconclusive and may not be recorded as PASS.
controls.remediation: Delete the key with `oci iam user api-key delete --user-id <ocid> --fingerprint <fingerprint>` (domain equivalent: `oci identity-domains api-key delete --endpoint <domain_url> --api-key-id <id>`). Move the automation that used it to a dedicated non-admin service user whose policy grants only the permissions the job needs, or better, to an instance/resource principal via a dynamic group. Keep human administrators to Console access with MFA, and give break-glass accounts no programmatic credentials at all.
controls.caveat: Checking only the group literally named Administrators is the classic false pass. Effective tenancy administrators also include any group a policy grants manage all-resources in tenancy (control 1.2 output feeds this check), dynamic groups with equivalent grants, and identity-domain principals holding the Identity Domain Administrator or Security Administrator application role, none of which appear in the Default-domain Administrators membership list. Each identity domain has its own Administrators group, so a multi-domain tenancy has several sets to enumerate — and the SCIM `members` attribute is not returned unless explicitly requested, so a collector that reads `groups list` output alone sees an empty membership and reports zero admins with keys. Use `fingerprint`, not `key-id`, as the key identifier: `key-id` is the composite tenancy/user/fingerprint string and will not be accepted by the delete command. Finally, a key on a federated admin is equally dangerous and equally invisible to legacy user listing.

controls.title: Attach a verified, monitored mailbox to every locally managed IAM account
controls.objective: Password resets, MFA enrolment, expiry warnings and security notifications are all delivered by email. An account whose address is missing, unverified, or points at a departed employee or a shared alias nobody reads cannot be recovered safely and cannot be warned when it is abused.
controls.procedure: Walk the compartment tree with `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all` (`--include-root` is a valueless switch; passing it a value aborts the command), resolve every identity domain URL with `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`, then run `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all --attribute-sets all` and inspect each user's `emails` array for an entry with `primary` true, checking its `value` and `verified` flags plus `active` and the federated-user flag. For the Default domain the legacy equivalent is `oci iam user list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all`, exposing `email` and `email-verified`. Then review each address against the current employee/contractor roster.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: Per user: the `emails[?primary]` entry's `value` and `verified` attributes from `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --attribute-sets all` (within `data.resources[]`), or `data[].email` / `data[].email-verified` from `oci iam user list`, keyed by user OCID and user name, alongside `active` and the federated flag.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every ACTIVE non-federated user has a primary email present and `verified` true, and the assessor has confirmed each address resolves to a mailbox owned by a current, identifiable owner. A user set drawn only from legacy `oci iam user list`, or a compartment walk that failed on the `--include-root` flag, is inconclusive rather than a PASS.
controls.remediation: Set or correct the address with `oci iam user update --user-id <ocid> --email <address>`, or in an identity domain with `oci identity-domains user patch --endpoint <domain_url> --user-id <id> --schemas '["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"]' --operations '[{"op":"replace","path":"emails","value":[{"value":"<address>","type":"recovery","primary":true}]}]'`, then drive the verification mail to completion. Point service and shared accounts at a monitored team distribution list rather than an individual, and add an offboarding step that reassigns or deactivates any account whose owner leaves.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because validity is a human fact, not an API field: the platform can prove an address was verified at some past moment, never that the mailbox is still monitored, still belongs to the named person, or is not a former employee's forwarded alias. A verified flag set two years ago is the most common false pass. Automated traps: legacy `oci iam user list` covers only the Default identity domain, so secondary-domain users are unassessed, and the domain discovery that would fix that depends on a compartment walk whose `--include-root` must be written without a value — the valued form errors out and an unchecked collector then reports zero domains and zero exceptions. Federated users often carry no OCI-side address at all because the attribute is mastered at the IdP; treating that null as a failure produces noise, while treating it as a pass hides genuinely unmanaged local accounts, so classify on the federated flag rather than on the null itself.

controls.title: Have workloads call OCI with instance or resource principals rather than embedded user keys
controls.objective: When compute instances, Functions and managed databases authenticate as an IAM user with a stored private key, that key sits on disk or in an environment variable, survives image cloning and backup, and cannot be revoked by terminating the host. Principal-based authentication issues short-lived, automatically rotated credentials bound to the resource itself.
controls.procedure: List dynamic groups with `oci iam dynamic-group list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all`, or per domain with the plural verb `oci identity-domains dynamic-resource-groups list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`, and record each `matching-rule`. Pull all policy statements across the compartment tree and select those whose subject is a dynamic group (remember the domain-qualified form `dynamic-group '<Domain>'/'<Name>'`). Inventory the workloads that call OCI with `oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query instance, functionsfunction, autonomousdatabase resources" --region <region>` for every subscribed region — the type name for a Function is `functionsfunction`, not `function`; the literal `function` is not an indexed Resource Search type, so a query using it either errors or silently returns no Functions at all. Confirm the exact type names with `oci search resource-type list` before pinning the query, and add `functionsapplication` if you want the parent objects. Map each workload to a matching rule, and separately flag non-human IAM users holding API keys.
api: oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query instance, functionsfunction, autonomousdatabase resources" --region <region>
controls.evidence: The `matching-rule` of each dynamic group from `oci iam dynamic-group list` / `oci identity-domains dynamic-resource-groups list`, the dynamic-group-subject statements from `oci iam policy get --policy-id`, the per-region workload inventory (`identifier`, `resource-type`, `compartment-id`) from `oci search resource structured-search`, and the API-key listing (`fingerprint`, `time-created`) for each suspected service user from `oci iam user api-key list --user-id`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when every workload in the per-region inventory that calls OCI APIs is covered by a dynamic group matching rule plus a policy granting it the access it needs, and no IAM user representing that workload holds an API key. An inventory built from a query containing an invalid resource type, or run in only one region, is inconclusive and may not be recorded as PASS.
controls.remediation: Create a dynamic group whose matching rule selects the workload (for example by instance OCID, compartment OCID, or resource type) and grant it access with `allow dynamic-group <name> to <verb> <resource> in compartment <name>`, using the domain-qualified subject form where the dynamic group lives outside the Default domain. Change the application to use the SDK's instance-principal or resource-principal provider, then delete the user's API key with `oci iam user api-key delete --user-id <ocid> --fingerprint <fp>` and, where the user existed only for that workload, delete the user.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because no OCI API can see inside the workload. The control plane shows that a dynamic group and policy exist; it cannot show whether the application actually uses the instance-principal provider or is still reading a private key from ~/.oci/config, a Kubernetes secret, or a Function configuration variable. Proving compliance requires host or source inspection. Two enumeration traps make the inventory silently short: the Resource Search type for Functions is `functionsfunction` (a query written with `function` returns no Functions, so the very resource class this control names disappears from the denominator and the check passes), and compute, Functions and databases are regional, so the inventory must loop every subscribed region while dynamic groups themselves are global. The domain-side list verb is the plural `dynamic-resource-groups list`. The mirror-image false pass: a service user holding an API key may be legitimate if the caller runs outside OCI, where instance principals are unavailable.

controls.title: Withhold delete permissions from delegated storage administrator groups
controls.objective: A storage administrator needs to create and configure buckets, volumes and file systems, but granting the full manage verb also grants destruction of the data and of its backups. Excluding the delete permissions from the grant means a compromised or mistaken storage admin cannot destroy the estate they operate, and keeps deletion as a separate, deliberately privileged act.
controls.procedure: Enumerate all ACTIVE compartments with `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all` (`--include-root` is a valueless switch — the valued form aborts the walk and leaves child-compartment policies unread). List policies in each compartment and read `statements` via `oci iam policy get --policy-id`. Select statements granting manage on `object-family`, `volume-family`, `file-family` (or the individual types buckets, objects, volumes, volume-backups, boot-volumes, file-systems, mount-targets) to any subject other than Administrators. For each, verify a `where all { ... }` clause excludes the family's delete permissions by name, and record the exact permission strings excluded. Enumerate the full permission list for each family from the service's policy reference before judging completeness, then compute the effective union of grants per principal by joining group membership (`oci iam group list-users --group-id <ocid> --all`) to every statement naming those groups.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: The verbatim statement from `oci iam policy get --policy-id`, showing whether it carries conditions such as `request.permission != 'BUCKET_DELETE'`, `!= 'OBJECT_DELETE'`, `!= 'OBJECT_VERSION_DELETE'`, `!= 'VOLUME_DELETE'`, `!= 'VOLUME_BACKUP_DELETE'`, `!= 'BOOT_VOLUME_DELETE'`, `!= 'FILE_SYSTEM_DELETE'`, `!= 'MOUNT_TARGET_DELETE'`, keyed by policy OCID and compartment OCID; plus the group membership listing used to build the effective per-principal union, and bucket retention-rule state as compensating evidence.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, for every non-Administrators principal, the union of all statements granting manage on a storage family carries conditions excluding every delete permission in that family — including the object-version and backup delete permissions, not only the parent object's — and no second statement or group membership restores deletion. A statement-by-statement evaluation that does not compute the per-principal union may not be recorded as PASS.
controls.remediation: Rewrite the grant with explicit exclusions, for example `allow group StorageAdmins to manage object-family in compartment X where all {request.permission != 'BUCKET_DELETE', request.permission != 'OBJECT_DELETE', request.permission != 'OBJECT_VERSION_DELETE'}`, with the volume equivalents (`VOLUME_DELETE`, `VOLUME_BACKUP_DELETE`, `BOOT_VOLUME_DELETE`, `BOOT_VOLUME_BACKUP_DELETE`, `VOLUME_GROUP_DELETE`, `VOLUME_GROUP_BACKUP_DELETE`) and the file-storage equivalents (`FILE_SYSTEM_DELETE`, `MOUNT_TARGET_DELETE`). Back this with bucket versioning plus retention rules and volume backup policies so that even an authorised delete is recoverable.
controls.caveat: Marked Manual because an assessor must judge completeness of the exclusion list, and an incomplete list is a silent false pass: excluding BUCKET_DELETE while leaving OBJECT_DELETE and OBJECT_VERSION_DELETE permitted still allows the contents to be destroyed, and excluding VOLUME_DELETE while leaving VOLUME_BACKUP_DELETE or BOOT_VOLUME_DELETE permitted destroys recoverability. Excluding the delete permissions is also not the same as preventing data loss — OBJECT_OVERWRITE (and unversioned buckets generally) lets the same principal replace object contents with no delete permission at all, so an exclusion list that stops at the DELETE strings should be paired with versioning and retention rules before it is called effective. The other trap is additive policy: OCI unions all grants, so a storage group that is also a member of a broader group, or is named in a second statement without conditions, regains delete — evaluate the effective union per principal, not each statement in isolation. Policies in child compartments must be walked, which requires `--include-root` written without a value.

controls.title: Dormant credentials are switched off rather than left latent
controls.objective: Dormant accounts and unused programmatic credentials expand the attack surface without serving anyone. They are rarely monitored, frequently belong to departed staff or retired automation, and are the credentials most likely to still be sitting in an old laptop image or repository. Deactivating them on a fixed idleness threshold shrinks that surface continuously.
controls.procedure: Per identity domain (compartment walk with `--include-root` as a valueless switch, then `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`), run `oci identity-domains users list --endpoint <domain_url> --all --attribute-sets all` and read the userState extension's last successful login date plus `active`. For non-console credentials, query the audit stream in every subscribed region against the subtree pseudo-log, not the root-only one: `oci logging-search search-logs --region <region> --search-query 'search "<tenancy_ocid>/_Audit_Include_Subcompartment" | summarize count() by data.identity.principalName, data.identity.credentials' --time-start <T> --time-end <T+chunk> --limit 1000`. Logging Search caps a single query's time range and returns a bounded page count, so split the 45-day window into chunks and paginate with `--limit`/`--page` inside each chunk before aggregating.
api: oci logging-search search-logs --region <region> --search-query 'search "<tenancy_ocid>/_Audit_Include_Subcompartment" | summarize count() by data.identity.principalName, data.identity.credentials' --time-start <iso8601> --time-end <iso8601> --limit 1000
controls.evidence: `urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:oracle:idcs:extension:userState:User.lastSuccessfulLoginDate` and `active` per user from `oci identity-domains users list`; and the per-credential `data.identity.credentials` occurrence counts from `oci logging-search search-logs` over the `_Audit_Include_Subcompartment` stream of each subscribed region for the last 45 days, joined to the credential inventories from `oci iam user api-key list` (by `fingerprint`), `oci iam auth-token list` and `oci iam customer-secret-key list`.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when (a) every ACTIVE user holding the console-password capability has a last successful login within 45 days — a null last-login on an ACTIVE account is a FAIL, not an exemption — and (b) every ACTIVE API key, auth token and customer secret key appears at least once in the `_Audit_Include_Subcompartment` stream of at least one subscribed region within the same window. IAM database credentials are excluded from test (b): they authenticate to the database listener and emit no OCI control-plane event, so their idleness is evidenced from database-side audit (Autonomous Database unified audit / DBA_AUDIT_TRAIL) or declared not evidenceable from OCI and routed to the manual procedure in 1.11.
controls.remediation: Deactivate an idle account by patching its `active` attribute to false in the identity domain: `oci identity-domains user patch --endpoint <domain_url> --user-id <id> --schemas '["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"]' --operations '[{"op":"replace","path":"active","value":false}]'` (for a legacy Default-domain user, remove credentials and group memberships instead). Reserve `oci iam user update-user-state --user-id <ocid> --blocked false` for clearing a lockout — it unblocks, it cannot deactivate. Then delete the idle credentials with the api-key, auth-token, customer-secret-key and db-credential delete commands. Automate this as a scheduled job driven by the audit query, and add an offboarding step that removes credentials on the day access ends.
controls.caveat: Four false results dominate. (1) `search "<tenancy_ocid>/_Audit"` returns root-compartment events only, so every credential used exclusively against resources in child compartments — nearly all of them — shows zero hits and is scored idle, while a genuinely idle credential in a sub-compartment-only tenancy is indistinguishable from a used one; the subtree pseudo-log `_Audit_Include_Subcompartment` is mandatory. (2) The audit stream is regional: a key used only from one region produces no events elsewhere, so loop `oci iam region-subscription list` rather than trusting the home region. (3) A never-used account returns a null last-login date; treating null as absence-of-evidence rather than a fail passes brand-new and long-abandoned accounts alike. (4) Only control-plane activity lands in `_Audit` — Object Storage S3/Swift data-plane traffic appears only if bucket read/write logs are enabled, and IAM database credentials never appear at all, so scoring them by audit silence manufactures FAILs on credentials in daily use and destroys confidence in the whole check. Logging Search also bounds both the query time range and the records per request, so chunk the 45 days and paginate or you will under-count usage. Finally, `update-user-state --blocked false` only clears a lockout; using it as the deactivation step leaves the account fully active.

controls.title: Allow no more than one active signing key per IAM principal
controls.objective: Each additional API key on a user is an independent, equally powerful credential that must be tracked, rotated and revoked. A second key that outlives a rotation is the copy nobody remembers — it keeps working after the 'current' key is replaced and is the credential most likely to remain valid on a decommissioned host.
controls.procedure: Against the home region, enumerate identity domains across the compartment tree (`oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all`, bare `--include-root`; then `oci iam domain list --compartment-id <id> --all`) and, for each domain, list every signing key in one call with the plural verb `oci identity-domains api-keys list --endpoint <domain_url> --all`, grouping by the `user` reference on each SCIM ApiKey. For the Default domain the legacy path is `oci iam user list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --all` followed by `oci iam user api-key list --user-id <ocid>` per user, grouping by `user-id`. Count keys in ACTIVE state per user and, for any user with more than one, record each key's `fingerprint` and creation timestamp — `key-id` is the composite `<tenancy_ocid>/<user_ocid>/<fingerprint>` string, not the fingerprint — so that a rotation in flight can be distinguished from a permanent second key.
api: oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --all --query 'data[].id' --raw-output
controls.evidence: A per-user count of ACTIVE API keys with each key's `fingerprint` and `time-created` (SCIM: `meta.created`), derived from `oci identity-domains api-keys list --endpoint <domain_url>` grouped by the `user` reference, or from `oci iam user api-key list --user-id <ocid>` grouped by `user-id`; `key-id` recorded only where the composite form is needed for cross-referencing.
controls.verdict_rule: FAIL when any user holds more than one ACTIVE API key and the older key's creation timestamp is more than 24 hours before the newest key's creation timestamp; otherwise PASS. Counting is done per identity domain, over ACTIVE keys only. A run whose user set came solely from legacy `oci iam user list` is inconclusive rather than PASS, because it omits every secondary domain.
controls.remediation: Decide which fingerprint is current, repoint every consumer to it, and delete the rest with `oci iam user api-key delete --user-id <ocid> --fingerprint <fp>` (domain equivalent: `oci identity-domains api-key delete --endpoint <domain_url> --api-key-id <id>`). If two keys are genuinely required for a make-before-break rotation, bound the overlap to the 24-hour tolerance the verdict allows and script the deletion of the superseded key as the final rotation step rather than leaving it for manual cleanup.
controls.caveat: A momentary second key during rotation is legitimate, which is why the verdict carries an explicit 24-hour overlap tolerance rather than a bare count — a rule that says 'more than one key is a FAIL' while the guidance excuses rotations makes the outcome depend on which text the assessor follows. Report the `fingerprint`, never `key-id`: the latter is the composite tenancy/user/fingerprint string, so grouping or deleting by it fails and cross-referencing to audit records breaks. Counting must be done per domain — the same human present in two identity domains is two distinct principals each entitled to one key, and merging them mis-reports in either direction — and the domain-side list verb is the plural `api-keys list`. Legacy `oci iam user list` returns only Default-domain users, so secondary-domain principals with several keys go entirely uncounted, and the compartment walk that finds those domains needs `--include-root` written without a value. Count only ACTIVE keys, and note the raw-request host differs by realm (oraclecloud.com, oraclegovcloud.com, and so on).

controls.title: Block internet-wide SSH reachability in VCN security list ingress rules
controls.objective: No VCN security list should let the whole IPv4 internet reach TCP/22, because a single permissive stateful rule exposes every instance in every subnet that list is attached to, turning SSH into a directly brute-forceable perimeter service.
controls.procedure: Resolve the region set with `oci iam region-subscription list --tenancy-id <tenancy_ocid>` and repeat everything below per region. Enumerate security lists tenancy-wide with `oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query SecurityList resources" --region <region> --all`, having first confirmed the type name is indexed in this tenancy with `oci search resource-type list --region <region>`. Because Search returns only what the caller can inspect, reconcile the count against the authoritative fallback walk: `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all` (`--include-root` is a valueless flag — passing it a value aborts the command; `--access-level ANY` rather than ACCESSIBLE so compartments the principal only sees indirectly are not dropped) then `oci network security-list list --compartment-id <c> --all --region <region>` per compartment. For each identifier run `oci network security-list get --security-list-id <ocid>` and evaluate ingress-security-rules. A rule fails when source-type=CIDR_BLOCK AND source=0.0.0.0/0 AND protocol is "6" or "all" AND any of: tcp-options is absent; tcp-options is present but destination-port-range is null (a tcp-options object carrying only a source-port-range leaves every destination port open, 22 included); or destination-port-range.min <= 22 <= destination-port-range.max evaluated numerically.
api: oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query SecurityList resources" --region <region> --all

oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all  # fallback walk; --include-root takes no value
oci network security-list list --compartment-id <compartment_ocid> --all --region <region>  # fallback when Search is unavailable or the caller is under-privileged
controls.evidence: The full ingress-security-rules array of each `oci network security-list get` response, keyed by security list OCID, vcn-id and compartment-id, quoting the offending rule object verbatim: source-type, source, protocol, is-stateless, and the whole tcp-options object including the explicit null/absent state of destination-port-range (recording "tcp-options present, destination-port-range null" distinctly from "tcp-options absent"). Record alongside it the per-region Search result count and the per-region compartment-walk count so a permission-truncated enumeration is visible in the evidence itself.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when, across every subscribed region, no security list has an ingress rule where source-type=CIDR_BLOCK AND source="0.0.0.0/0" AND protocol in {"6","all"} AND (tcp-options is absent OR tcp-options.destination-port-range is null OR destination-port-range.min <= 22 <= destination-port-range.max by numeric comparison). An enumeration that Search truncated relative to the compartment walk is not a PASS — it is an inconclusive result reported as a finding about the assessing principal's permissions.
controls.remediation: Rewrite the rule set with `oci network security-list update --security-list-id <ocid> --ingress-security-rules file://rules.json --force` (the update replaces the entire array and `--force` suppresses the overwrite prompt), replacing 0.0.0.0/0 with the operator CIDR and giving the rule an explicit tcp-options.destination-port-range rather than leaving it null, or delete the rule entirely and reach hosts through an OCI Bastion session or an on-prem-attached DRG/VPN path instead of a public SSH port.
controls.caveat: Five false-pass traps. (1) Resource Search is a regional endpoint with an eventually-consistent index — a single-region run, or a run seconds after a change, silently misses lists; and Search returns only resources the caller holds inspect on, so an under-privileged auditor gets an artificially clean set unless the compartment-walk reconciliation above is performed. (2) A tcp-options object that carries only a source-port-range has a null destination-port-range and therefore opens ALL destination ports; code that treats "tcp-options present" as "a port range was specified" passes the most permissive rule in the tenancy. (3) protocol "all" carries no tcp-options at all, so code that requires a destination-port-range object skips it. (4) The control text names only 0.0.0.0/0, but an ingress rule sourced from ::/0 is equally open — report it as an accompanying observation. (5) A security list attached to zero subnets still fails — do not filter on attachment; conversely a clean security list says nothing about the NSGs bound to the same VNICs, which is control 2.3.

controls.title: Block internet-wide RDP reachability in VCN security list ingress rules
controls.objective: No VCN security list should let the whole IPv4 internet reach TCP/3389, since publicly reachable Remote Desktop is a standing credential-stuffing and pre-auth-CVE target for every Windows instance in the attached subnets.
controls.procedure: Same traversal as 2.1 with the port changed. Per subscribed region (`oci iam region-subscription list --tenancy-id <tenancy_ocid>`), enumerate security lists via `oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query SecurityList resources" --region <region> --all`, and independently enumerate them through the fallback path — `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all` then `oci network security-list list --compartment-id <c> --all --region <region>` — reconciling the two counts before trusting an empty finding set. Then `oci network security-list get --security-list-id <ocid>` for each. In ingress-security-rules flag any entry with source-type CIDR_BLOCK, source 0.0.0.0/0, protocol "6" or "all", and tcp-options absent, or tcp-options present with a null destination-port-range (all destination ports open), or a destination-port-range numerically spanning 3389. Record compartment-id and vcn-id from the same response for reporting.
api: oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query SecurityList resources" --region <region> --all

oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all  # fallback enumeration; --include-root takes no value
oci network security-list list --compartment-id <compartment_ocid> --all --region <region>  # fallback enumeration, reconcile against Search
controls.evidence: The offending ingress rule object inside `oci network security-list get` output — source-type, source, protocol, is-stateless and the complete tcp-options object with destination-port-range min/max or its explicit null — plus the security list OCID, its vcn-id and compartment-id, and the per-region Search-count versus compartment-walk-count pair that proves the enumeration was complete.
controls.verdict_rule: PASS when no security list in any subscribed region has an ingress rule with source-type=CIDR_BLOCK AND source="0.0.0.0/0" AND protocol in {"6","all"} AND (tcp-options is absent OR tcp-options.destination-port-range is null OR destination-port-range.min <= 3389 <= destination-port-range.max by numeric comparison). A Search result count lower than the compartment-walk count makes the result inconclusive rather than PASS.
controls.remediation: Rewrite the rule set with `oci network security-list update --security-list-id <ocid> --ingress-security-rules file://rules.json --force` scoped to jump-host or corporate CIDRs and with an explicit destination-port-range, or drop the rule and front RDP with OCI Bastion or a DRG-attached private path.
controls.caveat: Beyond the 2.1 traps (regional and eventually-consistent Search, ::/0, protocol "all", unattached lists): a wide port range such as 1024-65535 or 3000-4000 contains 3389 without ever naming it, so a string match on "3389" produces a false pass — the comparison must be numeric containment. A tcp-options object whose destination-port-range is null is wider still and must fail. Search returns only resources the caller holds inspect on, so an under-privileged auditor gets an artificially clean result; the compartment-walk reconciliation above is the fix, and a Search count below the walk count is itself a finding about the assessing principal's permissions rather than a clean tenancy. Note also that RDP has a UDP transport on the same port number: a udp-options rule spanning 3389 from 0.0.0.0/0 is real exposure and should be reported as an accompanying observation even though the control names TCP.

controls.title: No security group exposes remote shell access to the whole internet
controls.objective: NSGs are applied directly to VNICs and are evaluated in addition to subnet security lists, so an NSG rule opening SSH to the internet exposes the attached instances even when every security list in the VCN is tight.
controls.procedure: Per subscribed region (`oci iam region-subscription list --tenancy-id <tenancy_ocid>`), get NSG OCIDs via `oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query NetworkSecurityGroup resources" --region <region> --all`, with the fallback walk `oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all` (`--include-root` is valueless; ANY rather than ACCESSIBLE so indirectly-visible compartments are not dropped) then `oci network nsg list --compartment-id <c> --all --region <region>`. Rules live outside the NSG object: call `oci network nsg rules list --nsg-id <ocid> --all --region <region>` and flag direction=INGRESS with source-type=CIDR_BLOCK, source=0.0.0.0/0, protocol "6" or "all", and tcp-options absent, or tcp-options present with a null destination-port-range (every destination port open), or a destination-port-range numerically covering 22.
api: oci search resource structured-search --query-text "query NetworkSecurityGroup resources" --region <region> --all

oci iam compartment list --compartment-id <tenancy_ocid> --compartment-id-in-subtree true --include-root --access-level ANY --lifecycle-state ACTIVE --all  # fallback walk; --include-root takes no value
oci network nsg rules remove --nsg-id <nsg_ocid> --security-rule-ids '["<rule_id>"]' --region <region>  # rule ids are opaque short strings, not OCIDs
oci network nsg rules update --nsg-id <nsg_ocid> --security-rules file://rules.json --region <region>
